fullDescription:
Ninety minutes feeding and bathing rescued elephants at the shelter outside Krabi Town.

The animals here came out of riding camps and logging work. The session is feeding first, then into the water with a brush. No riding, no chains during the programme, no performances. The elephants get in because they want to be in the water, and the keepers who work with them daily run the session rather than a rotating tour crew.

What you actually learn in ninety minutes is how to read an elephant: the condition of the feet, which carry several tonnes and are where most captive animals eventually fail; the skin behind the ears; how a relaxed trunk hangs. Once you know that, you can walk past any camp in Thailand and tell what kind of place it is, which outlasts the visit itself.

An honest caveat. Some welfare specialists argue that repeated bathing sessions with strangers are themselves a form of performance, and several of the best-regarded Thai sanctuaries have stopped offering them for that reason. This shelter runs them. If that sits badly with you, observation-and-feeding programmes exist in Krabi and are the better fit.

Also worth being clear about: Asian elephants in Thailand are almost entirely captive-bred or rescued. A shelter is a retirement arrangement, not a wild population, and the animals depend on people for food and veterinary care. Anywhere promising wild behaviour is overselling.

We book with the operator directly, so your place is held with them before your booking is final. The price covers hotel transfer, feeding and bathing with equipment, an English-speaking guide, coffee, tea, drinking water, seasonal fruit and photos.

Wear clothes you do not mind getting soaked. Ninety minutes, minimum one day's notice.
highlights: Rescued from riding camps and logging work
Feeding then bathing, no riding or performances
Run by the keepers who work with them every day
Learn to read any elephant camp you pass afterwards
Honest note: some sanctuaries now avoid bathing entirely

fullDescription:
The four islands on a power catamaran with clear-bottomed kayaks, which is a different day from the longtail version at a third of the price.

What the catamaran buys you is stability and space. Twin hulls do not roll the way a longtail does, there is a sun deck and netting to lie on, and the meal is served aboard rather than balanced on your knees on a beach. On a five-hour trip that is most of the experience.

The transparent kayaks are the part people book for. Paddling over shallow coral in a clear hull means seeing the reef without putting your face in the water, which matters if someone in your group will not snorkel, cannot swim confidently, or is travelling with small children.

Crew get in the water with you at the snorkelling stop rather than watching from the boat. That sounds like a detail and is not: on a busy reef with current, having someone in the water with the group is the difference between a relaxed swim and counting heads.

The route is the standard circuit, Poda, Chicken Island, Tup and Mor, with the Thale Waek sandbar walkable when the tide is low enough.

This is the version for comfort and for mixed-ability groups: anyone who will not snorkel still sees the reef through a kayak hull, and nobody spends five hours bracing against a roll.

We book with the operator directly, so your place is held with them before your booking is final. The price covers hotel transfer within Ao Nang and Krabi Town, the catamaran with crew, an English-speaking guide, a set meal and soft drinks, and snorkel gear.

Five hours. National park fees are collected at the pier unless confirmed otherwise. Minimum one day's notice.
highlights: Power catamaran, steadier than a longtail, with a sun deck
Clear kayaks let non-swimmers see the reef
Crew snorkel in the water with the group, not from the boat
Meal served aboard rather than on a beach
Comfortable enough for a full five hours aboard

fullDescription:
Three activities in two hours on the slope behind Ao Nang: canopy lines, an ATV track, and a roped climb on real limestone.

The climbing is the part worth coming for. Krabi's limestone is what made Railay one of the great sport-climbing destinations in the world, and the rock here is the same: pocketed, featured, and grippy in a way granite is not. Top rope means the rope runs from an anchor above you, so you are never more than a moment's slack from being held. Nothing needs upper-body strength; climbing is legs, and the instructors spend the session getting people to stop pulling with their arms.

The zipline runs between platforms built into the trees, at the height where tropical forest actually happens. The ATV section is on plantation and clay track, firm from November to April and properly muddy after the rains start.

A training session is included and is not a formality. All three activities are run with guides clipping and checking, and none of them assume prior experience.

Two hours is the short programme. There is a full-day version that includes a Thai lunch box; if you want the climbing to be more than a taste, that is the one to ask about, because two hours split three ways is about twenty-five minutes on the rock.

We book with the operator directly, so your place is held with them before your booking is final. The price covers round-trip transfer from Ao Nang, Ao Nammao or Krabi Town, the training session, fruit, bottled drinks and safety equipment. The Thai lunch box applies to the full-day programme only.

Wear closed shoes. Two hours, minimum one day's notice.
highlights: Top-rope climbing on the limestone that made Railay famous
Canopy zipline and an ATV plantation track
Training session included, no experience assumed
Two hours split three ways is a taste of each
Full-day version exists if you want real time on the rock

fullDescription:
Ten lines through the canopy in half an hour, including an 80-metre double line you can ride alongside someone.

Thirty minutes is short and the course is built for it: ten lines back to back with minimal walking between platforms, so the time is spent in the air rather than queueing on the ground. The 80-metre double is the long one, two cables side by side so two people leave the platform together, which turns the biggest line of the course into something shared rather than something you do alone and describe afterwards.

The high zip is the other named line and is exactly what it sounds like.

The platforms are set into forest on the slope behind the coast. The canopy is where most of the movement and noise in a tropical forest actually is, so the course puts you at the level worth being at, with limestone and coastline visible through the gaps.

Nothing here requires strength or experience. The harness carries you, guides clip and unclip at every platform, and the safety briefing is included. Closed shoes matter more than they sound like they should because the ground between platforms is uneven forest floor.

Thirty minutes makes this the thing you book around something else rather than a day's activity. It fits either side of a morning boat trip comfortably.

We book with the operator directly, so your place is held with them before your booking is final. The price covers the ten-course zipline, the safety briefing, fruit and water, and insurance. Transfers are not listed, so confirm how you are getting there when you book.

Minimum one day's notice.
highlights: Ten lines in thirty minutes, little walking between
80-metre double line ridden two at a time
Platforms at canopy height with coastline views
No strength or experience needed, guides clip you in
Short enough to fit either side of a boat trip

fullDescription:
The whole boat to yourselves, and a route you choose rather than one you join.

On a shared longtail you go where the schedule goes, you leave when the last person is back aboard, and you get twenty minutes at a beach you would have stayed at for an hour. A charter removes all of that. Pick Hong, Chicken Island or Phi Phi, and change your mind on the water if the sea or the crowds suggest it, because the skipper is working for your group rather than a manifest.

The practical gains are bigger than they sound. You can arrive at a stop before or after the fleet rather than with it. You can leave a busy beach immediately instead of waiting out the scheduled hour. With small children, you can go home early without negotiating it with twenty strangers.

The boat is fitted out beyond a working longtail: cushioned seating, a sun canopy, and a swim ladder, which is the detail that matters most because climbing back into an ordinary longtail over the side is genuinely awkward.

A picnic is set out on board, and a local skipper works with an English-speaking guide, so the person reading the water and the person explaining it are two different people who each do one job well.

At this price it makes sense for four or more sharing, or for anyone who has done the shared boat once and decided the schedule was the problem.

We book with the operator directly, so your place is held with them before your booking is final. The price covers private hotel pickup and drop-off, exclusive use of the boat, the skipper and guide, and the picnic meal.

Eight hours. National park fees are collected at the pier unless confirmed otherwise. Minimum one day's notice.
highlights: Whole boat to yourselves, no other passengers
Choose Hong, Chicken Island or Phi Phi, and change on the water
Arrive before or after the fleet instead of with it
Cushioned seating, sun canopy and a swim ladder
Makes sense from four people sharing upwards

fullDescription:
Five islands in seven hours on a longtail, weighted towards being in the water rather than looking at it.

The standard Krabi trip is four islands and a lot of moving between them. Adding a fifth and stretching to seven hours changes the balance: the stops get long enough to actually swim, and the snorkelling is treated as the point rather than a fifteen-minute box to tick.

Krabi's reef sits shallow and close to the islands, which is unusually forgiving. You do not need to be a strong swimmer or go out of your depth to see coral and reef fish; in several places you can stand up. Which stops are worth using on the day depends on the tide and how much wind has stirred the water, so the guide picks rather than following a fixed list.

The longtail is the slow boat and the right one here. Its shallow draught reaches water that speedboats have to anchor well away from, so you get dropped closer to the reef than a faster boat could manage.

Seven hours in open sun on an open boat is the thing to plan for. There is a canopy but the sides are open, and the reflection off the water burns people who thought they were in shade. A shirt you can swim in beats sunscreen you have to keep reapplying.

We book with the operator directly, so your place is held with them before your booking is final. The price covers hotel pickup and drop-off in Ao Nang, the longtail, a professional local guide, snorkelling equipment and a life jacket.

National park fees are collected at the pier unless confirmed otherwise, so carry cash. Minimum one day's notice.
highlights: Five islands over seven hours, so stops are long enough to swim
Shallow reef close to the beaches, forgiving for weak swimmers
Snorkel stops chosen on the day for tide and water clarity
Longtail gets dropped closer to the reef than a speedboat
Open boat: a swim shirt beats reapplying sunscreen
